# Is Exercise Equipment HSA Eligible? 3 Rules That Decide It in 2026 (Plus How to Buy a Rower Pre-Tax)


Last updated November 2026


Same rower either way. Whether HSA money can pay for it depends on why you're buying it.


**Short answer:** Sometimes. Exercise equipment is HSA and FSA eligible only when you buy it to treat a specific medical condition, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure or heart disease, and a licensed practitioner documents that in a Letter of Medical Necessity. Buying a rower to get in general shape doesn't qualify. If you do qualify, paying with pre-tax money cuts the real cost by roughly 20 to 40%.


If you're asking, you probably have a rowing machine open in one tab and an HSA balance in another. The rules are simpler than the internet makes them look: there are three, and they work the same for a rower, a treadmill or a bike. After the rules come the money math and a few real Aviron owners who bought a Strong Series for a health reason.


This is general information, not tax or medical advice. Rules vary by plan, so check with your plan administrator before you claim anything.


## In this article


- Is exercise equipment HSA eligible?
- What are the 3 rules that decide it?
- How much do you actually save?
- How do you buy a rower with HSA or FSA money?
- Who buys a rower for a health reason?

- FAQ


## Is Exercise Equipment HSA Eligible?


There's no official list of approved rowers and treadmills. The IRS cares about why you bought something, not what it is. Its rule for HSAs and FSAs comes from[Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) : medical expenses must be "primarily to alleviate or prevent a physical or mental disability or illness. They don't include expenses that are merely beneficial to general health."


Exercise helps nearly everyone, which is why it rarely counts. The IRS[FAQ on wellness expenses](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/frequently-asked-questions-about-medical-expenses-related-to-nutrition-wellness-and-general-health) says exercise for general health doesn't count "even if recommended by a doctor." A gym membership qualifies only when it's bought for "the sole purpose of treating a specific disease diagnosed by a physician (such as obesity, hypertension, or heart disease)." Home equipment follows the same logic.


So ask yourself whether you're buying the rower to treat something. The three rules below decide the answer.


## What Are the 3 Rules That Decide If Your Rower Qualifies?


### Rule 1: You Have a Specific Condition the Exercise Treats


The IRS's own examples are conditions where exercise is part of the treatment: obesity, diabetes, hypertension and heart disease. Truemed, the company that handles HSA/FSA checkout for Aviron, names hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obesity and depression on its[Aviron page](https://www.truemed.com/shop/partners/aviron) as conditions where Aviron is "especially beneficial."


"I want to get in shape before summer" doesn't count. Neither does "my doctor told me to exercise more" on its own.


### Rule 2: A Licensed Practitioner Puts It in Writing


That's the Letter of Medical Necessity, or LMN. It names your condition and explains why exercise on the equipment is part of treating it. Your own doctor can write one, or you can get one through Truemed at checkout: you fill in a private health survey, and a licensed provider reviews it.


In September 2026, the IRS showed how it judges a similar dual-use purchase when it added fitness wearables to that FAQ. The facts that count include "a recommendation from a medical practitioner" and your "symptoms, diagnosis, abnormal test results, or risk factors." It also says plainly: "A generalized desire to monitor or improve health is not sufficient." Your letter is how you show a rower purchase clears that bar.


### Rule 3: Your Plan Gets the Final Say, So Keep the Paperwork


An FSA administrator checks every claim, and IRS[Publication 969](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p969) requires a written statement from an independent third party showing the expense. An HSA runs on the honor system up front, but the IRS can ask questions later, and you "must keep records sufficient to show" the money went to qualified medical expenses.


Getting it wrong costs more with an HSA. A rejected FSA claim just means you pay with regular money. An HSA withdrawal that doesn't qualify is taxed as income, plus "an additional 20% tax" if you're under 65. Keep the receipt and the letter together, somewhere you'll still be able to find them in three years.


Rule 3 in real life: celebrate the workout, then file the receipt with your letter.


## How Much Do You Actually Save With HSA or FSA Money?


HSA and FSA dollars skip federal income tax. When they come out of your paycheck, they also skip the 7.65% Social Security and Medicare tax. What you save is simply your tax rate. Here's what that looks like on every $1,000 of qualified spending:


Federal tax bracket Plus payroll tax You save per $1,000


12% 7.65% $197


22% 7.65% $297


24% 7.65% $317


32% 7.65% $397


Before state income tax, which usually adds more. Social Security tax stops at an annual wage cap, so very high earners save 1.45% instead of 7.65% on the payroll part. HSA money you deposit yourself, rather than through payroll, gets the income tax break but not the payroll one.


That's where the "save about 30%" on HSA/FSA checkout pages comes from: a 22 or 24% bracket plus payroll tax. According to Aviron's[HSA/FSA page](https://www.avironactive.com/truemed/) , the annual membership can qualify too.


### What It Costs Per Workout


The number that decides whether a rower was worth it is what each workout costs you, and that depends far more on you than on the tax code:


For every $1,000 of machine Regular money Pre-tax money (22% bracket)


Used 3 times a week for a year (156 workouts) $6.41 per workout $4.51 per workout


Used 3 times a week for 3 years (468 workouts) $2.14 per workout $1.50 per workout


Used twice, then it becomes a clothes rack $500 per workout $351.50 per workout


The tax break saves about 30%. Using the machine for three years instead of twice cuts the cost per workout by more than 99%.


### 2026 Limits and Deadlines


For 2026, you can put up to $4,400 in an HSA with self-only coverage, or $8,750 with family coverage. HSA money never expires, and you can reimburse yourself years later for a qualified purchase made after the account was opened.


A health FSA tops out at $3,400 in 2026 and is use-it-or-lose-it at the end of the plan year. Your plan may offer a grace period of up to 2 1/2 months or let up to $680 carry over, but not both. One FSA perk matters a lot for a big purchase: your whole annual election is available from day one of the plan year, before it has come out of your paychecks. If you're picking next year's amount during open enrollment, plan around that. Not sure which account you have? Our[HSA vs FSA guide](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/hsa-vs-fsa-fitness-equipment/) lays out the differences.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can I use my HSA to buy a rowing machine?


Yes, if you're buying it to treat a diagnosed condition and you have a Letter of Medical Necessity. Without those, a rowing machine is a general fitness purchase and doesn't qualify. If you qualify, you can buy Aviron's rowers, treadmills and bikes with HSA or FSA money through Truemed.


### Did the new tax law make gym equipment HSA eligible?


No. An earlier version of the 2025 tax bill would have let HSAs reimburse some sports and fitness costs, but that provision didn't make the final law, according to[HUB International's benefits bulletin](https://www.hubinternational.com/products/employee-benefits/compliance-bulletins/2025/07/obbbas-impact-on-employer-benefits/) . Fitness groups are still lobbying for a standalone bill, the PHIT Act. Until something passes, the Letter of Medical Necessity route is the only one.


### Is the Aviron membership HSA eligible?


It can be. Aviron's HSA/FSA page says qualified customers can use pre-tax HSA or FSA money on the annual membership as well as the rower, through the same Truemed process.


### What happens if I use my HSA on something that doesn't qualify?


The withdrawal counts as taxable income, and if you're under 65 you also owe an additional 20% tax, according to IRS Publication 969. That's the main reason to have your letter in hand before you swipe the HSA card.


### Can I spend leftover FSA money on a rower before the year ends?


Yes, if you qualify and the purchase falls inside your plan year or its grace period. Many plan years end on December 31, but check yours. The letter has to come first, so give yourself a few days, not a few hours.
